deep.reconstruction:
The page belongs to Grothendieck's 1983 Teichmüller notes. The previous page lists the elementary 'Lego' surfaces Σ_(0,3), Σ_(0,4), Σ_(1,1) with their modular dimensions d. The next page counts cells in hexagon and square decompositions and their double covers. This page links three things: pants decompositions, maps (dessins) and real curves.

(1) The main text reads: 'Carte cellulaire (pas orientée) com[pacte/connexe] dont tous les sommets sont d'ordre 3 (ou 1) <-> cartes cellulaires triangulées ≃ revêtements de P^1_C ramifiés seulement en 0,1,∞'.
- In modern terms: a not-necessarily-oriented map whose vertices all have valency 3 or 1 is, by duality, the same as a triangulated map, where valency-1 vertices give folded triangles.
- In the oriented case these are the finite coverings of P^1_C unramified outside {0,1,∞} with the appropriate ramification constraints. Equivalently they are coverings of the modular j-line, i.e. Belyi pairs, i.e. dessins of 'clean triangular' type.

(2) Combinatorial encoding. A map is a set of flags with three involutions σ0, σ1, σ2: change the vertex, edge or face of the flag. The relations σ0^2 = σ1^2 = σ2^2 = (σ0σ2)^2 = 1 define the cartographic group C_2.
- Adding (σ0σ1)^3 = 1 forces the <σ0,σ1>-orbits to have order 3 or 1. With the Esquisse convention, faces are <σ0,σ1>-orbits, so this gives triangles; dually, vertices of order 3 or 1.
- The resulting group <σ0,σ1,σ2 | σi^2, (σ0σ2)^2, (σ0σ1)^3> is the extended (2,3,∞) triangle group, i.e. PGL_2(Z), the extended modular group.
- Its orientation-preserving index-2 subgroup is PSL_2(Z) = Z/2 * Z/3. The '±' written near a loop presumably refers to this orientation sign / PSL_2 vs PGL_2.
- So finite trivalent unoriented maps correspond to finite PGL_2(Z)-sets, and oriented ones to finite PSL_2(Z)-sets, i.e. coverings of the j-line.

(3) Boundary and real curves.
- 'σ0, σ1, σ2 sans pts fixes' is the condition that the map has no boundary and no free half-edges.
- 'R-courbes algébriques' (replacing a struck 'variétés algébriques') records that unoriented maps correspond to real algebraic curves / Klein surfaces. The orientation double cover is a complex curve with an antiholomorphic involution, the reflections σi lifting complex conjugation.
- The base segment 0—1 (the trivial dessin [0,1] ⊂ P^1) is drawn as the reference object.

(4) The pair of pants figure. Boundary circles A, B, C carry marked points aB, aC, bA, bC, cA, cB. These are the 'seams' joining each pair of boundaries, as in the later Lego–Teichmüller formalism.
- Identifying the pants with P^1 − {0,1,∞}, the real line cuts it into upper and lower half-planes. These are two triangles with vertices 0, 1, ∞, i.e. two hexagons after truncating the cusps.
- So the seams are the real segments, and a pants decomposition with seams is a hexagon (= truncated triangle) decomposition. That is exactly a triangulated map dual to the trivalent graph of the decomposition, carrying a canonical real structure.
- The thickened trivalent graph drawn in the centre (double lines) is the ribbon-graph picture of this. The sketches illustrate small maps: a tetrahedron (triangulated sphere, dual to K4), a lollipop with a valency-1 vertex, a one-vertex map on the torus, a figure-eight, a circle with 3 marked points, and a cycle of circles (a degenerate maximally-split curve).

(5) The next page counts hexagons/edges/vertices of such decompositions and of their double covers. This is the bookkeeping for building the Teichmüller tower from these pieces.
errors: No mathematical error visible. Note a convention issue: with Grothendieck's Esquisse convention (σi changes the i-th component of a flag), (σ0σ1)^3 = 1 constrains faces to order 3 or 1, i.e. it describes the triangulated side of the duality, not the trivalent side directly. The page's '<->' makes the duality explicit, so this is consistent.

'revêtements de P^1_C ramifiés seulement en 0,1,∞' is a slight imprecision for the trivalent case. Trivalent maps correspond to coverings with ramification indices dividing 3 over one point and 2 over another (the j-line with points 0, 1728, ∞), not to arbitrary Belyi covers. Arbitrary Belyi covers correspond to arbitrary (bipartite/clean) maps, or to triangulations via the barycentric subdivision.

missed.claim: The page juxtaposes three structures: pants decompositions with seams (hexagon decompositions), trivalent unoriented maps given by three involutions, and real algebraic curves. It suggests that a pants decomposition with seams is a 'real' trivalent map: the degenerate curve made of copies of P^1 − {0,1,∞} with their real structures. This idea is implicit in Ihara–Nakamura and Lego–Teichmüller work, and is essentially standard, but its explicit formulation as an unoriented-map / real Belyi object is not prominent.
missed.quote: σ0^2=σ1^2=σ2^2=(σ0σ2)^2=(σ0σ1)^3=1 … R-courbes algébriques … σ0,σ1,σ2 sans pts fixes
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Minor. It frames the base points of the Teichmüller tower as real trivalent maps. This could connect real-structure (complex conjugation) actions on the Grothendieck–Teichmüller tower to the combinatorics of PGL_2(Z)-sets, but this is largely known in spirit.

deep.surprise_reason: The content is the cartographic group, PGL_2(Z) for trivalent maps, the duality with triangulations and Belyi covers, and maps on non-orientable surfaces as real curves. All of this appears in the Esquisse or in Jones–Singerman / Bryant–Singerman. The pants-with-seams figure is standard Lego–Teichmüller material. The only mildly interesting feature is the explicit juxtaposition with real curves in the Teichmüller context.
